title: Is lipid goal one-size-fits-all: A review of evidence for recommended low-density lipoprotein treatment targets in Asian patients.
text_summary: 本综述探讨了亚洲人群中LDL-C治疗目标"一刀切"策略的适用性。比较了东西方人群在血脂代谢、饮食结构、他汀药代动力学和心血管风险特征方面的差异，提出亚洲患者可能需要更低的LDL-C阈值和不同的治疗策略，为亚太地区血脂管理指南的制定提供了循证依据。
text:
Review
Is lipid goal one-size-fits-all: A review of
evidence for recommended low-density
lipoprotein treatment targets in Asian
patients
Yun Wang1, Bryan P Yan2, Brian Tomlinson3 and
Vivian WY Lee4
Abstract
The international guideline recommendations for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) lowering were made
based on the results of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), meta-analyses, and observational studies mostly in the
White population. It was not clear whether these LDL-C targets could be applicable to other ethnic groups, for example,
Asian patients. This review aimed to address major aspects related to the lipid goal and statin therapy in Asia, including
the epidemiology of cardiovascular disease, the LDL-C profiles, the lipid goals from localized guidelines, genetics and
lifestyles, and the efficacy and safety of statins. Owing to the geographic, ethnic, genetic, and cultural diversity in this
region, we observed a geographic pattern of diversity in cardiovascular epidemiology and statin response in Central Asia,
East Asia (particularly for Asia-Pacific region), and South Asia. The rapidly growing literature from Asian countries
questioning ‘‘lower is better’’ hypothesis was noticed. However, owing to the nature of these dominantly observational
data, the conclusion was hardly confirmative. Despite the rapid expansion of the current literature in this region, efforts
should be made to ensure an adequate sample size to assess the significance of a given lipid parameter on overall
cardiovascular outcomes in this Asian population.
Keywords
lipid-lowering, statins, lipid goal, Asia, cardiovascular
Received 16 January 2019; accepted 19 March 2019
Introduction
The
existing
literature
has
consistently
suggested
the ‘‘lower is better’’ hypothesis1 regarding the correl-
ation between cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk and
low-density
lipoprotein
cholesterol
(LDL-C)
level:
the lower the LDL-C, the better the outcome. The
lipid-lowering agents, especially 3-hydroxy-3-methyl-
glutaryl coenzyme A reductase inhibitors (statins),
lower
patients’
lipid
level
and therefore
improve
the long-term outcomes in CVD patients,2 and the
initiation of statin treatment has been recommended
by international guidelines3,4 as a secondary prevention
strategy for recurrent future atherosclerotic cardio-
vascular disease (ASCVD). The National Cholesterol
Education
Program
Adult
Treatment
Panel
III
(NCEP ATP III)5,6 recommended a lipid goal of
<2.6 mmol/L
(<100 mg/dL)
among
preexisting
ASCVD patients. The updates to the ATP III guideline
in 2004 (also known as ‘‘2004 ATP III updates’’)6 set up
a lower LDL-C level of <1.8 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) in
the highest-risk patients based on evidence from the
emerging
randomized
controlled
trials
(RCTs).

The American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American
Heart Association (AHA)4 published new guidelines in
2013 on the management of cholesterol levels. This
guideline was no longer following the prior ATP III
guidelines to target very speciﬁc lipid goals. It empha-
sized the administration of high-potency statin (or
moderate-potency statins for patients above 75 years)
therapy instead of ‘‘treat to target’’ goals for LDL-C
levels. The concept of ‘‘lower is better’’ for LDL-C
levels was replaced by the a ‘‘more is better’’ approach
to statin therapy. The 2016 European Society of
Cardiology (ESC)/European Atherosclerosis Society
(EAS) guidelines7 made it clear that an LDL-C goal
of <1.8 mmol/L should be achieved or at least 50%
reduction of the baseline LDL-C level if it was between
1.8 and 3.5 mmol/L in very high-risk patients. The 2017
American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists
(AACE)/American College of Endocrinology (ACE)
guidelines8 highly recommended a more stringent lipid
goal of <55 mg/dL (1.42 mmol/L) for extreme high-risk
patients, namely progressive ASCVD patients after
achieving an LDL-C level of <70 mg/dL, established
clinical CVD in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM),
chronic kidney disease (CKD), or heterozygous familial
hypercholesterolemia (HeFH); and patients with a his-
tory of premature ASCVD (<55 male and <65 female).
The 2018 updated ACC/AHA guideline9 was built on
the 2013 cholesterol recommendations of statin therapy
with a focus on addressing the importance of lifestyle as
the ‘‘risk enhancers.’’
However, the guideline recommendations3,4,7,8 were
made based on the results of RCTs, meta-analyses,
and observational studies that mostly recruited White
patients, with the JUPITER trial being the only statin
trial that enrolled signiﬁcant numbers of Black and
Hispanic participants.10 It was not clear whether these
target LDL-C goals could be applied to other ethnic
groups, for example, Asian patients, and achieve equiva-
lent clinical beneﬁts when compared with White patients.
The Asia region referred to countries in Central Asia,
East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Paciﬁc
Islands in this review. Given that countries in this region
had a wide diversity of ethnicities, the existing literature
targeting this population was rare. It may be diﬃcult to
outline the cardiovascular epidemiology of all the coun-
tries in this region. This review aimed at addressing
major aspects related to lipid goal and statin therapy
in selected countries in the region.
Epidemiology of CVD in Asia
Probably due to the ethnic, geographic, and economic
diversity in this region,11 we observed a geographic pat-
tern of cardiovascular epidemiology in Central Asia,
East Asia (particularly for Asia-Paciﬁc region), and
South Asia. As the proportion of total deaths from
CVDs in 2016, the mortality was highest for both
males and females in Central Asia, next highest in East
Asia,
and
lowest
for
high-income
South
Asia12
(Supplementary Table 1). Although a dramatic drop in
mortality owing to CVD was observed worldwide,13
most Asian countries, except for Taiwan (24.20%),
South
Korea
(24.92%),
Myanmar
(23.40%),
Cambodia (24.52%), and Thailand (21.86%), saw a sub-
stantially higher death rate attributable to CVD than in
Western countries,11,14 of which China (41.12%) was
amongst the highest (Supplementary Table 1). In par-
ticular, some East Asia and Southeast Asian countries,
for example, China, Vietnam, North Korea, South
Korea, and Cambodia demonstrated a stroke-dominant
pattern (Supplementary Table 1): there were twice as
many deaths from stroke as from ischemic heart disease
(IHD).11 Blood pressure was believed to be a more
important determinant of the high prevalence of stroke
in East Asians, rather than LDL-C level.15,16 In consid-
eration of the potential clinical beneﬁts of lowering sys-
tolic blood pressure to below 115 mmHg,17 there is a
growing need for the lifestyle modiﬁcation, antihyperten-
sive treatment, and home blood pressure monitoring to
help manage hypertension in Asians.18
Lipid guidelines in Asia
Only a few East Asia and South Asia countries have
their local cholesterol management guidelines such as
China, Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines (Table 1).
The
2015
Clinical
Practice
Guideline
of
the
Philippines19 recommended that high-potency statins
were recommended to lower LDL-C by >30% or to
<70mg/dl in the primary and secondary prevention of
ASCVD, both for diabetic and non-diabetic patients. In
the most recently updated 2016 version of the Chinese
guidelines,20 people who were diagnosed with ASCVD
were directly listed as a very high-risk population. The
lipid goal for very high-risk Chinese patients was low-
ered
from
<2.0 mmol/L
(80 mg/dl)
in
2007
to
<1.8 mmol/L
(70 mg/dl)
in
2016,
although
some
researchers insisted on not changing the target value of
<2.0 mmol/L.21,22
In
Hong
Kong,
the
lipid
goal
for preexisting CVD patients was set at 1.8 mmol/L
(70 mg/dl).23 Taiwanese guidelines24 believed that lipid-
lowering therapy in peripheral arterial disease (PAD)
was controversial. The LDL-C target in these patients
should be <100 mg/dL and optimally <70mg/dL if
there was the coexisting presence of coronary artery dis-
ease (CAD). The lipid goal in the 2012 Japanese guide-
line25 was to guarantee that the LDL-C goal of
<100 mg/dL or 20–30% reduction should be achieved
for ASCVD patients. Given the high coronary heart
disease (CHD) risk in Indian people, the Indian
2

guidelines26 promoted a more stringent lipid goal of
<50mg/dL as a safe strategy. However, most Asian
guidelines were relying on observational studies and clin-
ical experience to generate the recommendations. Owing
to the lack of existing clinical trials, it was not a surpris-
ing fact that most Asian guidelines were lacking the ade-
quate support of RCTs.27 However, it came to our
attention that the lipid goal of 50% LDL-C reduction
from high-potency statins as recommended in 2013
ACC/AHA guidelines probably received high reluctance
in Asian guidelines and from local clinical practice.28
Lipid-lowering therapy
Although the current guidelines emphasized that low-

important, questions still remained about the selection
of statin intensity/potency in diﬀerent ethnic popula-
tions. Some of the existing pharmacogenetic studies29,30
showed that genetic variations in the cytochrome
P450 (CYP450) enzymes and solute carrier organic
anion transporter, could be the major contributor
to the ethnic diﬀerence in statin response and side
eﬀects. The genetic polymorphism that might inﬂuence
statin pharmacokinetics included adenosine tripho-
sphate-binding
cassette
transporters,
CYP7A1,
P-Glycoprotein, apolipoprotein E protein, cholesteryl
ester transfer protein, proprotein convertase subtilisin/
Kexin type 9, and atrogin-1.30
Prescribing statins for primary and secondary pre-
vention of CVD was widely promoted as a global trend
during the past decade,31 and Asia was no exception.
When statin prescribing decreased the CVD risk on a
population scale, the beneﬁts to each individual patient
should be weighed against the risks. The commonly
reported adverse eﬀects related to statins32 were the
increased risk of diabetes, myopathy, elevated liver
enzymes, cataracts, fatigue, and decreased sexual func-
tion.
Chan
et
al.33
analyzed
the
existing
Pﬁzer-
sponsored atorvastatin clinical trials that began in/after
1992 and were completed before 2012. They drew the
conclusion from 52 short-term trials and 6 long-term
trials that the incidence of (serious) adverse events with
atorvastatin 10–40 mg in Asian patients was low. The
adverse events of the higher dose (80 mg) of atorvasta-
tin were hardly conclusive owing to the limited number
of Asian patients (n ¼ 28) who received this dose.
However, their study population was a pooled popula-
tion of East Asian, Oriental, South Asian, and Paciﬁc
Islander participants. In some certain populations, for
example, the Chinese population, the situation could be
more complicated. The intensive statin dosing scheme
met the great challenge in the mainland Chinese guide-
lines,20 yet there was no solid data to verify the con-
taminated eﬀect owing to the high-intensity statin in
any Chinese clinical trials. Atorvastatin was the typical
statin that always raised the debate; however, the
review article34 that searched the literature in PubMed
using the keyword ‘‘atorvastatin’’ found there were
no signiﬁcant diﬀerences between Chinese and non-
Chinese population in term of pharmacology and
clinical eﬃcacy and safety of the atorvastatin. In
another retrospective cohort study35 based on 19,033
Chinese matched by propensity score to 57,099 non-
Chinese old patients (mean age ¼ 74 years) who were
newly prescribed statins in Ontario, Canada between
2002 and 2013, researchers did not ﬁnd the higher
risk of serious statin toxicity in Chinese, in terms of
hospitalization with rhabdomyolysis, incident diabetes,
and acute kidney injury, and all-cause mortality, than
non-Chinese older adults with similar indicators of
baseline
health
proﬁles.
Another
clinical
trial
DISCOVERY (DIrect Statin COmparison of LDL-C
Values: an Evaluation of Rosuvastatin therapY) Asia
study36 found the identical safety proﬁles of rosuvasta-
tin 10 mg and atorvastatin 10 mg in the Asian popula-
tion, which was consistent with Whites.
Although the toxicity of aggressive statin remained
unclear, the retention of high-intensity statin seemed
acceptable because the clinical beneﬁts of high-intensity
statin over the standard dose were still not justiﬁed. The
results from the Intensive Statin therapy for Chinese
patients with Coronary Artery disease undergoing
Percutaneous coronary intervention (ISCAP) trial37
that examined 1202 patients with stable angina or
non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome
(NSTE-ACS) found intensive statin treatment (80 mg
atorvastatin daily  2 days before percutaneous coron-
ary intervention (PCI) and 40 mg daily  30 days after
PCI) did not improve the primary endpoint, in terms of
incidence of major adverse cardiac events (MACEs),
including cardiac death, myocardial infarction (MI),
and unexpected target vessel revascularization, within
30 days after PCI compared with usual care, but led to
similar safety proﬁle (the incidence of contrast-induced
nephropathy
(CIN),
alanine
transaminase
(ALT)/
aspartate transaminase (AST) >3  upper limit of
normal (ULN), creatine kinase (CK) >5  ULN).
The CHina Intensive Lipid Lowering with statins in
Acute
coronary
Syndrome
(CHILLAS)
trial,38
a
nationwide, prospective, and open-label trial carried
out in 20 clinical centers in China, found the intensive
dose of statin (atorvastatin, 20 or 40 mg/day, moderate-
to high-potency statin, n ¼ 680) brought an incremental
LDL-C reduction of 6.4%, compared with lower dose
of statin (atorvastatin 10 mg/day, low-potency statin,
n ¼ 675), but it did not result in any reduction of pri-
mary endpoints throughout the 2-year follow-up,
including cardiac death, non-fatal acute MI (AMI),
revascularization with either PCI or coronary artery
bypass graft (CABG), ischemic stroke, documented
unstable angina, and severe heart failure. In the just
presented
but
not
yet
published

(EMPATHY)
study,39 5, 042 non-CHD patients who had high
LDL-C levels and were diagnosed with diabetic retin-
opathy in Japan were randomized to either the stand-
ard therapy, which aimed at an LDL-C level of 100–
120 mg/dL, or intensive lipid-lowering therapy with a
target at <70 mg/dL. Throughout a follow-up of 37
months, the intensive statin group did not have lower
incidence of cardiac events (hazard ratio (HR) ¼ 0.84,
p ¼ 0.15), but was associated with a reduction in the
secondary endpoint of cerebral events (cerebral infarc-
tion
or
cerebral
revascularization)
(HR ¼ 0.52,

p ¼ 0.01), particularly cerebral infarction (HR ¼ 0.54,
p ¼ 0.02).39
Whether the situation in East Asia should also apply
to South Asians, a population at higher risk for CHD,
could raise further questions. As reported previously,
Asian Indians40 could achieve a higher plasma level
(1.68 times) given 40 mg of rosuvastatin compared
with Whites. Data from the PRospective Assessment
of Cardiovascular risk and Treatment In Canadians
of varying Ethnicity (PRACTICE) study41 from 86
South Asians and 137 Whites indicated that atorvasta-
tin 20 mg/day and simvastatin 20 mg/day modulated
LDL-C
and
high-density
lipoprotein
cholesterol
(HDL-C) levels to a similar degree in both South
Asians and Whites with documented CHD. These ﬁnd-
ings may imply that South Asian patients could be
treated with atorvastatin and simvastatin at the same
doses which were typically applied to White patients.
The Investigation of Rosuvastatin in South Asian
Subjects (IRIS) trial42 also supported that the 10 and
20 mg doses of rosuvastatin and atorvastatin were well
tolerated and could achieve the guideline-recommended
LDL-C reduction in South Asians.
Most clinicians were aware that Asians might
respond diﬀerently from Whites in pharmacokinetic
and pharmacodynamic eﬀects of statins. These diﬀer-
ences remained stable43 even after adjustment for the
potential confounding factors, such as age, gender
comorbidities, and socioeconomics. When deciding
whether or not to add the ‘‘more’’ statin therapy,
there should be a signiﬁcant shift in the focus from
the idea of eﬃcient achievement of the lipid goal to a
further justiﬁcation of pharmacokinetics and pharma-
codynamic sensitivity to statins in Asian patients.44
Genetics and lifestyles
Variations in lipid proﬁles among diﬀerent ethnic
groups are likely due to a mixture of factors, for exam-
ple, genetics and lifestyles. Some of the abnormal chol-
esterol levels that were common in South Asians were
likely due to the genetic proﬁle. Genetic variation
in linkage disequilibrium with the XbaI and ins/del
polymorphisms of the apo B gene contributes to the
determination
of
total
cholesterol
and
HDL-C
levels.45 In the 1979–1993 data of the Canadian
Mortality Database, South Asians, which included
India and Pakistan, tended to be present with high
cause-speciﬁc death rates from IHD compared with
Chinese people.46 In a study that compared lipid
levels among South Asians and Europeans,47 the
mean triglyceride levels among South Asians and
Europeans were 1.96 and 1.54 mmol/L (p < 0.0001),
respectively,
and
HDL-C
levels
were
1.01
ver-
sus 1.19 mmol/L , respectively (p < 0.0001), despite
the
relatively
comparable
LDL-C
(3.33
versus
3.15 mmol/L, P < 0.02) and total cholesterol (5.21
versus 5.04 mmol/L, p < 0.04) levels. Abdominal obes-
ity, which was more prevalent in South Asians than
Whites, could contribute to the elevated cholesterol
levels in South Asians and further lead to a higher risk
of CVDs.48 The high risk of CVD and mortality in
Indian people, as a typical example of South Asians,
represents a paradox scenario. The ‘‘Indian paradox’’
scenario49 was deﬁned as a dilemma in which Indian
people in their countries or after migration suﬀered
from an excess burden of heart diseases, although the
conventional risk factors such as smoking, obesity,
hypertension,
and
hypercholesterolemia
were
not
higher in Indians compared with Whites.50-52 Some
researchers identiﬁed the contributing factors as insuﬃ-
cient physical activity and unhealthy food;53-55 however,
the traditional risk factors could not fully explain the
Indian
scenario.
The
emerging
novel
risk
factors
included ‘‘coronary artery calcium score, lipoprotein
(a),
apolipoproteins,
homocysteine,
thrombosis
markers plasminogen activator inhibitor 1, carotid
intima-media
thickness,
genotypic
variations,
non-
alcoholic fatty liver disease, C-reactive protein, platelets,
birth weight levels’’56 and the undernutrition in early life
followed by overnutrition in adult life.57
Yet in some countries of East Asia, for example,
China and Japan, there was another story. Compared
with North Americans and Europeans, Chinese58,59 and
Japanese60 patients reported having superior statin
responsiveness and lower LDL-C levels. The plasma
levels of statins in Japanese patients were higher and
the half-life of the statins was longer after a given dose
of any statin.61 This was found in other Asian coun-
tries, but was best studied in Japan and China.61 The
ﬁnding held true even after adjustment for body
weight61 and was, therefore, probably the key reason
why Japanese tended to use lower doses of statins, for
instance, atorvastatin 40 mg/day instead of 80 mg/
day.62 It was speculated that the diﬀerences in the
LDL-C
response
to
statins
between
Asians
and
Whites
were
yielded
by
the
diﬀerential
pharmacokinetics40,63 and genetic proﬁle.64,65
Some researchers attributed the lower LDL-C values
in East Asians to diet.66,67 However, one recent study in
Singapore that involved Chinese, Malays, and Indians
suggested that the dietary or genetic factors, if taken
separately, could hardly explain ethnic diﬀerences in
the lipid proﬁles.68 In recent years, the risk proﬁle of
East Asians may be related to the increasing prevalence
of novel risk factors such as high rates of smoking and
diabetes in this area.69 Asia has undergone rapid eco-
nomic development since the 1950s accompanied by
urbanization, migration, and a westernized lifestyle
(such as high intake of dietary saturated fat and
Wang et al.
5


decreased physical activity70). Japanese researchers
constantly recorded the negative impact of the western-
ization of lifestyles.71,72 The fat intake in Japanese
migrants to the United States lied between the native
Japanese and native Americans, and their cholesterol
levels were higher than those of native Japanese despite
the stable death rate from CAD.71 The Ni-Hon-San
study73 published in 1975 looked at Japanese residents
in Japan, Honolulu, and San Francisco, and found that
the LDL-C levels increased as the population moved
east across the Paciﬁc. They concluded the dietary-
induced lifestyle should be the main contributor to
the diﬀerences between Japanese people living in
Japan and San Francisco. Among South Asians, deep
frying and overcooking of food was widely practiced,
which probably put South Asians at a high CVD risk
associated with the saturated and trans fats generated
from the food processing.74 Similarly, China reported
increasing levels of total and LDL-C cholesterol attrib-
uted to the modern dietary patterns.70,75 Singapore
used to report higher levels of total cholesterol and
LDL-C than China76, but their LDL-C levels have
dropped dramatically in recent years,77 whereas the
prevalence of dyslipidemia in Hong Kong and Taiwan
was lower still. A higher ratio of unsaturated against
saturated fats in the diet was identiﬁed as the reason for
the lower rates of dyslipidemia in these two countries.76
Interestingly, immigration or westernization was
regarded as a blessing rather than a curse to South
Asians. In the literature, researchers believed the accul-
turation to western lifestyles brought a higher variety
and quality improvement to the dietary practice of
South Asians living in Canada and the USA.78,79
However, Asian Indian vegetarians and non-vegetar-
ians shared a similar pattern of dyslipidemia and simi-
lar rates of CVD.80 Indian immigrants to the UK had
lower total and saturated fat consumption (38.8% and
13.7% of energy consumed) when compared with the
local population (42.2% and 18.5%, respectively), but
the coronary death rate was still 40% higher.81 If the
CVD risk in the Indian population did not decline upon
immigration to foreign countries, a genetic factor was a
possibility while the lifestyle also fueled the excessive
risk of CVD.82
Rethinking LDL-C goal and statin therapy
in Asia
There was a rapidly growing literature from Asian
countries, questioning the ‘‘the lower (the cholesterol
levels) the better (clinical outcomes)’’ hypothesis. In a
recent analysis of cholesterol goals published in April
2015,83 the relationship between all-cause mortality and
cholesterol levels in Japanese was unique: mortality
actually went down with higher total cholesterol or
LDL-C levels. In this report, the researchers believed
the theory ‘‘lower is better’’ was completely wrong for
Japanese patients and put forward the concept of a
‘‘Japanese paradox’’: Japanese people had high choles-
terol
levels
with
very
low
mortality
from
AMI.
This report raised the discussion: was there a J- or
U-shaped curve for East Asian patients regarding the
correlation between the lipid level and clinical out-
comes? The Ibaraki Prefectural Health Study84 was
one of the studies to support this, in which a total of
30,802 men and 60,417 women, with no history
of stroke or CHD, were followed for 10 years. The
U-shaped correlation between the all-cause mortality
and LDL-C levels was identiﬁed in men, with lowest
mortality rate with LDL-C between 120 and 139 mg/dL
and the highest mortality rate with LDL-C <80 mg/dL,
whereas among women CHD deaths increased slowly
with LDL levels.
The observations in other Asian regions echoed the
Japanese ﬁndings. The main ﬁnding85 from 13,473
AMI patients in a large-scale Korean Myocardial
Infarction registry found that achieved target LDL-C
levels <70mg/dL (1.8mmol/L), regardless of statin ther-
apy, were not associated with a lower risk for cardiovas-
cular events as compared with non-achievers. In another
recent Korean study,86 obtaining a  50% reduction in
LDL-C was associated with better clinical outcomes after
AMI, whereas achieving the <1.8mmol/L goal was not.
The results from the large-scale Japanese Coronary
REvascularization
Demonstrating
Outcome
study87
with 14,866 patients who underwent the ﬁrst coronary
revascularizations identiﬁed that the risk for MACEs
was signiﬁcantly higher in the 120mg/dL group than
the 80–99 mg/dL group, but was not signiﬁcantly lower
in the <80 mg/dL group. In Chinese patients, Hong
Kong researchers88,89 observed the clinical beneﬁts asso-
ciated with the lipid goal attainment of <2.6 mmol/L
through one-year follow-up, but not for the goal of
<1.8mmol/L and  50% reduction. In 402 Chinese MI
patients,88 they found that LDL-C goal attainment
of <2.6 mmol/L resulted in a signiﬁcant reduction in
mortality (10.8% versus 24.2%, p¼ 0.001), but not for
goal attainment of <1.8mmol/L. In a larger sample of
1684 post-PCI ACS patients, attainment of an LDL-C
goal of <2.6mmol/L was signiﬁcantly associated with
lower rates of MACEs during the one-year follow-up,
and those who achieved the LDL-C level of 1.8mmol/
L did not seem to carry any incremental clinical beneﬁts.
Even in Central Asia, the population-based study using
data from 31,619 IHD patients in Israel concluded that
patients with LDL-C levels of 70–100 mg/dL had lower
risk of MACEs compared with those with LDL-C levels
at 100–130 mg/dL, but they failed to observe any add-
itional beneﬁt in the patient group achieving LDL-C
<70mg/dL.

South Asians, mainly Asian Indians and who have
ancestral origins in the Indian subcontinent (for exam-
ple, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Nepal90),
were historically identiﬁed as a special group with one
to two times increased morbidity and mortality from
CVD.91 The reasons appeared to be multifactorial,
including but not limited to the diet, obesity, genetics,
and a unique lipid proﬁle.9 Unfortunately, this minority
population was barely represented in clinical trials, and
a conservative management plan was required with
stricter goals as well as an aggressive therapy for this
special population.90
Discussion
Deﬁning who was ‘‘Asian’’ in this speciﬁc discussion
should raise attention when considering health out-
comes and cardiovascular epidemiology. There was a
great diversity in biological and genetic proﬁles across
the Asian ethnicities, and the common aggregation of
the ‘‘Asian’’ population might mask the diﬀerences in
the lipid proﬁles, statin responses, and lipid targets.
South Asians had a unique lipid proﬁle that might pre-
dispose them to a high prevalence of CHD, character-
ized by elevated levels of triglycerides, low levels of
HDL-C, elevated Lp(a) levels, and a higher atherogenic
particle burden despite relatively normal or slightly
higher LDL-C levels;90 however, the conventional risk
factors might not fully explain the increased CHD
risk in this population. East Asian maintained a rela-
tively lower cholesterol level compared with White
patients,92-94 as reported in the international study
Dyslipidemia
International
Study
II
(DYSIS
II).
Central Asia faced a signiﬁcantly larger burden of
CVD linked to the conventional risk factors, elevated
blood
pressure,
high
total
cholesterol,
obesity/
overweight, and smoking,95 as compared with the
other regions of Asia. In this region almost 70% of
stroke deaths occurred owing to high blood pressure,
whereas in East Asia and South Asia the high blood pres-
sure led to 50% of stroke deaths.95 In the presence of the
diverse geographic and ethnic patterns, the loose classiﬁ-
cation method of ethnic ‘‘Asian’’ had limitations and
failed to embrace the heterogeneity in this region.
Moreover, the current lipid treatment thresholds
were mostly extrapolated from Western guidelines
owing to the paucity of evidence-based data in Asian
populations. Despite the rapid expansion of the current
literature in this region, eﬀorts should be made to
ensure adequate sample sizes to assess the signiﬁcance
of a given lipid parameter on the cardiovascular out-
comes. RCTs remain a challenge in many Asian coun-
tries because most of these countries failed to follow the
International
Conference
on
Harmonization/Good
Clinical Practice (ICH/GCP) guidelines.96 Japan is
probably one of the best countries to oﬀer a well-
developed environment for clinical trials, because
patient recruitment in Japan is eﬃcient.97 However,
these existing RCT studies still have several limitations,
including small sample sizes, low study quality, short
study duration, and the use of surrogate endpoints
instead of hard clinical endpoints. The variation in
the classiﬁcations of endpoint events and the inclusion
criteria of patients made it virtually impossible for us to
compare between the studies.
Varying deﬁnitions of composite and surrogate
endpoints, such as MACEs, can lead to substantially
diﬀerent results and conclusions.98 Therefore, when
composite study endpoints (for example, MACE)
should be used, researchers are highly recommended
to construct individual study endpoints to match with
other relevant research aiming for the same clinical
goals. In RCTs, endpoints are pre-speciﬁed, whereas
the endpoints in observational studies can be deﬁned
as a posteriori during or after the conduct of the
study.99 The observational cohort study has its advan-
tage over the clinical trial by examining long-term
clinical outcomes but is restricted by real-world clinical
care,
making
it
incompatible
with
the
standard
endpoint assessment in clinical trials. In observational
studies, various endpoints should be included, such as
hard endpoints, soft endpoints, surrogate endpoints,
and patient-reported endpoints,99 or it will be more
helpful if the observational studies restrict their focus
to appropriate, and valid straightforward ‘‘hard’’ clin-
ical endpoint, such as cardiovascular-related mortality,
and individual endpoints, instead of surrogate and
composite endpoints. Therefore, it is important to
standardize the classiﬁcation of what should be the
most straightforward ‘‘hard’’ clinical endpoint as the
pre-deﬁned criteria for the endpoint event.100
Conclusion
Owing to the geographical, ethnic, genetic, and cultural
diversity in Asia, the one-size-ﬁts-all lipid recommenda-
tions seem less practical. The challenge remains for
individual countries to implement clinical trials in
local populations to validate international guidelines.
Further research may emphasize the development of
local scenarios incorporating the local evidence and
the available new lipid-lowering treatments.
